title: AI UGC Video Ads Guide: What Makes One Work | AIVideosUGC
description: UGC means a clip that looks like a creator made it. Make one from a photo or a product link, with words, a voice, and a person on screen. Not a real customer.
h1: AI UGC Video Ads Guide: Creator-Style Clips for Your Shop
lead: A UGC ad should feel like a person talking about the item, not a studio spot. Start from a photo of what you ship, or from the public listing. You still read the line before it goes out.
secondary_keywords: short video ads for small brands
summary: How a shop turns one product photo, or the public listing, into a short ad that sounds like a person talking.

sections.h2: What Counts as an AI Video Ad?
paras: You leave with a short ad you can post, from a photo or the public listing. Nobody has to visit the storeroom with a camera.

Publish it on [Instagram](page:plat-instagram), [Facebook](page:plat-facebook), or [TikTok](page:plat-tiktok). A feed post can be square at 1:1. A full-screen story wants 9:16. 16:9, 4:3, and 3:4 are available when the placement asks for them.
sections.alt: Hands hold plain gray skincare jar beside a bathroom mirror and open its lid.

sections.h2: See What a Creator-Style Ad Looks Like
paras: A tall clip fills a phone, a square file sits in a scrolling post, and a wide file fits a larger screen.
The pictures use one jar so you can see the hand, the lid, and the room. Your file should do the same: the product is already in motion in the opening beat.
sections.alt: Hands choose between two views of plain gray skincare jar on a bathroom shelf.

sections.h2: Reasons to Make Video Ads Here
paras: Written from what you sell. If the blanket is queen size, the line can say queen size.
Ready for a placement you pay for. A Reels placement wants the sneaker tall. A feed post can take the same shoe as a square. Ask for 9:16 or 1:1, and use 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4 when that placement asks.
More than one style in a run. One cut can whisper about the knit of a scarf. Another can show the fold with no speech. Keep the one that matches the scarf you sell.

sections.h2: How to Make a Video Ad With AI in 3 Steps
paras: Name the action first, such as a hand lifting the lid. Then paste the listing, or type one sentence about who the jar is for.
You get a clip back with someone speaking. The line can say how the cream sits on the skin, which is something you can show.
Save the file and put it in the ad account you already use for that jar. If the placement is a story, use the tall file. If it is a feed, use the square one.
Paste the listing in [URL to video](page:url-to-video), or choose the face in the [actor library](page:ai-actors). A second opening is another job from the same photo.
sections.alt: Hands scoop a small amount from plain gray skincare jar onto a hand.

sections.h2: What a Shop Gains From AI Video Ads
paras: A full ad without a shoot. The person who usually emails a creator can instead start from the product photo on the page. There is no call time to set.
A monthly plan instead of a creator day rate. [See the plans on the pricing page](page:pricing). Three openings are three separate jobs.
More versions from one product. The next test can change only the first sentence, or only the room. It is a new job, so you decide if that test is worth the credits.
A fresh cut when the old one has been in market. If the comments all quote the same opening joke, write a new one about the stitching instead. The product photo can stay as it is.
You stay in charge. Tell it the brand sounds calm, and write the offer you are actually running. The words on screen can match the words you approved.
You can run it as an ad. A finished clip on a paid plan can go into paid placements, and it has no watermark.
Short product videos and photo tools live in the [video toolkit](page:video-hub).
Ads that sit with a store listing: [Shopify](page:plat-shopify).
Frames for the feed and for Reels: [Instagram ads](page:plat-instagram).

Describe the ad and let [AI video ads](page:video-ads) finish the file.
Rebuild a look you already like from the [template gallery](page:templates).
Speed. You start from a still or a listing address instead of booking a crew.
Cost. Those three jobs draw from the credits on your plan. You are not collecting a new quote for each opening line.
More versions. Another hook is another clip, not another day on a set.
You keep the brief. The line uses the words the brand already says, and you can export again after a change.
Rights. A finished file on a paid plan can run as an ad.
The next product. Repeat the same path on the next item.
Different shops put the same kind of file to work in different ways.
A tea shop keeps the tin in a hand from the first beat to the last, then checks the lid against the real tin.
A home shop lets the person who packs orders make the spoken ad, as long as they can photograph the cushion in daylight.
A gadget seller approves a still of the real charger before anyone asks for a clip of it in a hand.
A jewelry seller changes the price on the necklace clip in the same project, so the caption matches the tag on the tray.
A supplements seller keeps the tub in frame and records a second spoken line for the country the next shipment goes to.
A clothing seller skips the studio booking and makes test files from a photo of the clothes.
A fashion shop uses an avatar for a launch and keeps the line on the clothes.
A food seller builds a new table scene for each flavor from pack photos, then a short spoken ad.
A store owner starts from the product page only after the photo of the tote is the one customers receive.
A decor shop tells the project the lamp must stay off until the last second, then watches that the shade color survived.

sections.h2: What Should the Clip Start With?
paras: Open on the product already doing something, with the item already in a hand.
For a travel mug, show the lid twist, a sip, or the mug held up. One action per clip. Ten seconds has room for that moment and a glimpse of the room.
sections.alt: Hands pull plain gray skincare jar from a tote onto a bathroom counter.

sections.h2: How Long Should the Ad Be?
paras: Use 6 or 10 seconds for one action, 15 when the product has to be used, and 30 for a fuller showing. Pick 9:16 so the clip fills the phone.

Six seconds is a lid coming off and costs 24 credits. Ten seconds fits that action plus a second look and costs 40. Fifteen can take the product out, use it, and set it down, and costs 60. Thirty leaves room for a longer showing and costs 120. You see the number before you start.

Use 1:1 for a square scrolling post, 16:9 for a wide screen, and 3:4 or 4:3 when the placement asks for that shape. Each length or shape is a new clip. For a clip of the product in use, start with [product videos](page:product-videos).
sections.alt: Hands close plain gray skincare jar on a neutral bedroom dresser.

paras: The file includes the spoken line, captions, and music you are allowed to run in an ad. Read the captions before you publish, and fix a wrong word before the ad goes live.

Put the words in the upper middle of a tall video, away from the app buttons at the bottom and the right edge. Use a face from the actor library and a logo you own. The [Content Policy](/content) says what can be uploaded.

sections.h2: Can I Present the Avatar as Someone Who Bought It?
paras: No. The face is generated, so the line stays on the product and how it is used.
Make another version when you want a different room or a different first action.
You can post from a product photo or the public listing, at 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. Read the line before you post.
A finished clip can run in ads.

faq.q: What does a video-ad tool build for a shop?
faq.a: A short ad for a product you already sell. You bring the photo or the listing, and you get a file with someone speaking. The guide walks your shop through each step.

faq.q: How do I build the ad?
faq.a: Start with a product photo. Say the first action is the lid coming off. Download the tall file if the ad is a story, or the square file if it sits in the feed.

faq.q: Who is an AI video ad tool for?
faq.a: A shop that needs an ad for each product it sells this month. It is a poor fit when you only want one filmed founder story.

faq.q: Do I pay before the first ad?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits.

faq.q: Can I run the file as a paid ad?
faq.a: Yes. A paid plan is what lets you put the file in an ad account, and the download has no watermark.

faq.q: Which shapes and platforms can I use?
faq.a: Wherever the ad runs. [YouTube Shorts](page:plat-youtube-shorts) and [TikTok](page:plat-tiktok) want a tall 9:16 file. A square 1:1 file can sit on [Facebook](page:plat-facebook) or [Instagram](page:plat-instagram). 16:9, 4:3, and 3:4 are there when the placement names them.

faq.q: Can I make ads for many products?
faq.a: Yes. Run a batch across the products you choose. Each clip shows its credit cost before it starts. If a job fails, those credits come back.

faq.q: Do these stand in for a creator?
faq.a: Use a generated clip for the product that needs three openings this week. If buyers only trust the founder, film the founder for that one product and use generated clips for the others.

faq.q: Will TikTok, Facebook, or Instagram reject the ad?
faq.a: These apps do not ban a generated ad as a category. They do care if the clip pretends a stranger bought the product. Read that app's current ad rules before you spend, and read our [Content Policy](/content) for what you can upload.

faq.q: What if the clip shows a part my product does not have?
faq.a: Make the clip again and name the exact action and the exact product in the sentence.
